references.text: Moses wished to see God's glory, and God let His glory pass before him. Peter's desire to remain on the mountain reflects this wish to stay in the nearness of God's glory.
The Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot), where Israel was to dwell in huts/tents. Peter's suggestion to build three huts can be linked to this feast and its significance as a reminder of God's presence.
The parallel passage in Matthew where Peter suggests building three huts for Jesus, Moses, and Elijah during the transfiguration on the mountain.
The parallel passage in Mark where Peter suggests building three huts. Mark explicitly adds that Peter did not know what to say, for they were terrified.
Peter calls Jesus 'Master' (Epistata), the same form of address used here in 9:33, which shows Peter's consistent reverent approach to Jesus.
The immediate context where Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up the mountain, and Moses and Elijah appear in glory – the background for Peter's statement.
Peter himself refers back to the transfiguration on the mountain as a testimony to Jesus' majesty and glory, which he was an eyewitness to.
The Word became flesh and 'tabernacled' (pitched His tent) among us – Peter's wish to build huts/tents reflects the theme of God's presence dwelling among people.
God's dwelling (tent/tabernacle) among humanity – the final fulfillment of God's presence among His people, which Peter, in his eagerness, wished to realize already on the mountain.
